note: Per-match tactical breakdowns. Fields under `grounded` come from FotMob's match data and are never written by the LLM. Fields under `explained` are model commentary constrained to that data. `conceptsTaught` drives the lesson curriculum so it ramps instead of repeating.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went to Napoli, took control of the ball and spent most of the night camped in Napoli's half, but couldn't find a way through for over an hour. Napoli barely attacked at all — five shots all match, no corners — and relied on their goalkeeper, who made six saves. Martin Ødegaard finally settled it on 75 minutes, finishing an assist from Christos Tzolis, and it ended 1-0 to Arsenal.
explained.opponentPlan: Napoli matched Arsenal's 4-2-3-1 on paper but played it very differently: Allegri's side conceded the ball (42% possession) and defended deep and compact, accepting territory in exchange for keeping bodies between Arsenal and their goal. The numbers show it clearly — Napoli made 14 tackles to Arsenal's 9 and had only 126 passes in the opposition half, so they were defending and clearing rather than building. Arsenal's answer was volume and width: 433 passes in Napoli's half, 51 touches in the box and 26 shots, working the ball side to side until a gap appeared, while Napoli's total lack of a counter-attacking threat (0 big chances) meant Arsenal could keep committing bodies forward without much risk.
explained.keyMoment: The 75th minute, Ødegaard's goal from a Christos Tzolis assist. Until then the pattern was total Arsenal control with no reward — 26 shots and 6 saves from the Napoli goalkeeper tell you how long the door stayed shut. The goal didn't change the shape of the game so much as finally cash in the shape of the game that had existed since kick-off, and it came from a captain arriving in the box rather than from the wide players who had been doing most of the crossing.
explained.nerdCorner: The gap between xG 4.05 and xGOT 1.69 is the real story, and it's a different story from the one the scoreline tells. xG asks "how good was the opening?"; xGOT asks "how good was the shot once it left the boot?" — it only counts efforts that reached the goal. So Arsenal generated four goals' worth of openings and delivered under two goals' worth of on-target attempts, with 26 shots but only 8 on target. That is a finishing/shot-selection shortfall, not a chance-creation shortfall, and it's the more encouraging of the two problems to have: chance creation is a repeatable team process, whereas conversion at this volume regresses toward the mean fairly quickly. The flip side of the trade-off: sustaining 433 passes in the opposition half against a side that offers nothing on the break (0 big chances, 5 shots) is comparatively cheap. The interesting question is whether the same shape holds up against an opponent who actually punishes a high, committed back line.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal lined up 4-2-3-1, but a back four with the ball usually becomes a back three: one full-back (typically Ben White on the right) tucks in alongside the centre-backs while Piero Hincapié pushes high up the left touchline. That leaves two holding midfielders — Declan Rice and Mikel Merino — screening in front, and five players spread across the last line to stretch the opponent's defence as wide as possible. When Arsenal lose the ball, Hincapié drops back in and the wide attackers fall into a flat line, so the shape reverts to two banks of four with Viktor Gyökeres and Martin Ødegaard nearest the ball.

lesson.explain: Picture the pitch cut into five vertical lanes: two touchlines, the central lane, and the two lanes in between — those in-between lanes are the half-spaces. They matter because a defender standing there doesn't know whether he belongs to the centre-back or the full-back, so a runner arriving in that lane is often nobody's problem until it's too late. That is exactly the territory a No. 10 like Ødegaard lives in, and it's why 51 touches in Napoli's box came from a team facing a deep, compact defence: when the middle is packed and the touchlines are covered, the half-space is the only lane left to attack. His 75th-minute finish is the archetype — the ball goes wide to Tzolis, the defence shifts toward the touchline, and the goal comes from someone arriving between the lines rather than from a straight run through the centre.
lesson.spotIt: Watch Ødegaard when Saka has the ball on the right touchline — he'll drift into the gap between Napoli's right-back and their nearest centre-back, and that patch of grass is the half-space.

statTranslations.plain: From the quality of chances created, a typical night with this pattern of play ends with Arsenal scoring around four and Napoli scoring nothing — so 1-0 flatters Napoli enormously.

The chances were worth roughly four goals, but the shots that actually reached the goalkeeper were only worth about 1.7 — meaning a lot of good openings were skewed wide or blocked rather than being saved.
Arsenal created five clear openings and Napoli created literally none — this was not a game that could plausibly have gone the other way.

statTranslations.stat: Shots inside box 15 vs 2, touches in opposition box 51 vs 8
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal weren't just having more of the ball, they were having it in the most dangerous 18 yards of the pitch, which is the difference between sterile possession and genuine pressure.
Napoli's night was pure containment — their keeper was their most active attacking-phase contributor and they never once forced Arsenal to defend a set piece.

explained.whatHappened: Chelsea scored almost immediately — Morgan Rogers finished a Jorrel Hato pass in the 2nd minute — and Arsenal spent the rest of the match chasing the game they were already better in. Kai Havertz levelled it on 25 minutes from a Declan Rice pass, and five minutes into the second half Martin Ødegaard put Arsenal ahead after Christos Tzolis set him up. Arsenal had 16 shots to Chelsea's 13, but 13 of Arsenal's came from inside the box, and Chelsea's goalkeeper had to make 8 saves to keep the score that close.
explained.opponentPlan: Xabi Alonso's 3-4-2-1 is built to be hard to play through — three centre-backs, a flat four in midfield, and two forwards tucked just behind the striker — and it gives you an extra man at the back to defend against Arsenal's five-across-the-front. Chelsea got their reward inside two minutes through Rogers, then had a lead to protect, and the numbers show what that turned into: Arsenal 54% possession, 267 passes in the opposition half to Chelsea's 191, and 44 touches in the Chelsea box against 26. Arsenal's answer was not to force it through the middle of those three centre-backs but to keep arriving in the box from wide and from the second line — 13 of their 16 shots came from inside the area, and Chelsea created zero big chances all match against Arsenal's four.
explained.keyMoment: Ødegaard's goal on 50 minutes, assisted by Tzolis. Arsenal had already equalised through Havertz on 25 and had spent the rest of the first half with the ball; scoring so soon after the restart meant Chelsea, who had been defending a lead in a five-at-the-back shape, now had to come out and chase. From there Arsenal never conceded another big chance — Chelsea finished the match with zero — while Chelsea's keeper ended up making 8 saves.
explained.nerdCorner: The scoreline hides how lopsided the chance quality was: Arsenal's xG on target was 2.0 against a total xG of 2.05, meaning almost everything they generated actually forced a save rather than being blocked or dragged wide — that is unusually clean finishing volume, and it's why the Chelsea keeper's save count reached 8. Chelsea's profile is the mirror image: 13 shots but only 5 inside the box, 0.39 xG and zero big chances, which is the signature of a team that has a lead, sits in a back five, and takes what it can get from range. Note too that Chelsea won the tackle count 12-10 while Arsenal won interceptions 9-7 — tackles are what you make when the ball is already being carried at you, interceptions are what you make when you've read the pass, and that small split is consistent with Chelsea defending their own third while Arsenal squeezed the game higher up (267 passes in the opposition half to 191).

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal lined up 4-2-3-1, but a back four with Riccardo Calafiori at left-back rarely stays a flat four when Arsenal have the ball. Calafiori typically steps forward or inside while Ben White tucks in alongside Ezri Konsa and Gabriel, which leaves three defenders at the back, two holders in Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly in front of them, and five attackers across the last line — Saka, Ødegaard, Havertz, Tzolis and whoever pushes up from full-back. When Arsenal lose the ball those five drop back into two banks of four with two players nearest the ball, which is what people mean by a 4-4-2 mid block.

lesson.explain: A transition is the five or ten seconds right after the ball changes hands, before either team is organised again — and it is when most goals are scored, because defenders are out of position. Chelsea's goal on 2 minutes is the purest example: that early in a match nobody has settled, Hato found Rogers, and it was 1-0 before Arsenal's shape existed. The rest of the match shows the flip side — once both teams were set, Chelsea managed 13 shots but only 5 from inside the box and zero big chances, because chances against an organised defence come from further out and at worse angles. Arsenal's two goals, from Rice to Havertz and Tzolis to Ødegaard, came from a team that had the ball 54% of the time and kept walking into the box: 44 touches in there, 13 shots from inside it.
lesson.spotIt: The instant Arsenal lose the ball, count to five and watch how many red shirts are sprinting back rather than towards the ball — that count tells you whether Arsenal are trying to win the transition or survive it.

statTranslations.plain: Chelsea never once got into a genuinely good scoring position after the second minute — their goal came from the one moment nobody was organised.
Both teams shot a similar number of times overall, but Arsenal were shooting from good places and Chelsea mostly weren't.
The quality of chances says this should have been roughly a two-goal Arsenal win, which is exactly what happened — the 2-1 is not a fluke.
Chelsea's keeper had twice as much work to do, which is usually the clearest sign of who spent the match under pressure.

statTranslations.stat: Touches in opposition box: Arsenal 44 | Chelsea 26
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal got into the dangerous area far more often, not just once or twice in a lucky spell.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal had the ball for most of the afternoon at Villa Park and spent the first hour probing without breaking through. Bukayo Saka finally scored on 59 minutes, set up by Riccardo Calafiori. Villa had as many shots as Arsenal — seven each — but not one of them hit the target, and David Raya finished the game without making a single save.
explained.opponentPlan: Villa lined up in the same 4-2-3-1 as Arsenal, which means every Arsenal player had a natural opponent in front of them — a mirror match. Unai Emery's side conceded the ball willingly (39% possession) and defended by making contact: 20 tackles to Arsenal's 13, but only 2 interceptions to Arsenal's 8. That is the profile of a team reacting to the ball rather than reading passes ahead of time. Arsenal's answer was volume and patience in Villa's half — 237 passes there against Villa's 147, and 21 touches in the opposition box — pushing Villa deeper and deeper until a gap opened on the hour.
explained.keyMoment: The 59th minute: Calafiori to Saka, 1-0. In a mirrored 4-2-3-1 the game had been stuck for an hour — every Arsenal player marked by his opposite number — and the breakthrough came from the one player whose starting position doesn't match anyone's: the left-back arriving high on the far side of the pitch to feed the right winger. Everything after it was game management, and Villa's response amounted to zero shots on target all match.
explained.nerdCorner: The scoreline says 1-0 and the shot count says 7-7, but the honest number is xGOT 0.8 to 0.0. Villa managed seven attempts and did not put one on target — Raya recorded zero saves. That is not luck; it is what happens when a team has to shoot from wherever the ball squirts loose rather than from positions they built. The interception split (8-2) is the tell underneath it: Arsenal were intercepting passes, which means they were positioned in the passing lanes before the ball moved, while Villa's 20 tackles show a defence arriving after the fact. A tackle-heavy, interception-light profile is usually a team that is reacting rather than anticipating — it keeps you in a game, but it hands the opponent the tempo. On these numbers, 1-0 flatters Villa more than it flatters Arsenal.

shape.plainEnglish: A 4-2-3-1 is just the starting positions; it is not where players stand once the ball is moving. With this personnel Arsenal usually slide one full-back inside or push the other high, so the back four becomes a back three with two midfielders screening in front — and five attackers spread across the last line. Calafiori is typically the player who causes that shift, stepping infield or advancing from left-back, which is exactly the kind of position from which a left-back ends up creating a goal.

lesson.explain: An overload just means getting more players into one area of the pitch than the opponent has defending it. Villa played the same 4-2-3-1 as Arsenal, so on paper every man was matched — and that is precisely why the game was goalless for an hour. The way you break a mirror match is to add a body from somewhere the opponent isn't counting: Arsenal's 237 passes in Villa's half were the process of shifting Villa across and pulling an extra player into one zone, and the goal on 59 minutes came with Calafiori — a defender, not a forward — supplying the pass. That is a numerical advantage created not by having better players in a spot, but by having one more.
lesson.spotIt: When Arsenal have the ball near a touchline, pause and count Arsenal shirts versus opponent shirts in that corner of the screen — if Arsenal have one more, watch how quickly the ball gets played into the box from there.

statTranslations.plain: Villa shot as often as Arsenal but never once forced Raya to make a save, so the equal shot count is misleading — the quality gap was total.
Arsenal created two genuinely good openings and Villa created none; the chances Villa did take were the difficult, hopeful kind.
Once you only count shots that actually hit the goal, Villa's attacking output rounds to literally nothing.
Arsenal defended by reading and stepping in front of passes; Villa defended by chasing and lunging after the pass had already arrived.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in the opposition half 237 vs 147
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal spent the game camped in Villa territory, which is why Villa's seven shots never came from good positions.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal took control early and never gave it back: Kai Havertz scored on 15 minutes from a Riccardo Calafiori pass, and Bukayo Saka made it two on 23. Four minutes into the second half Martin Ødegaard added a third, set up by Ben White. Arsenal had 20 shots to Coventry's 4 and kept a clean sheet, with David Raya making just one save all afternoon.
explained.opponentPlan: Coventry set up in a matching 4-3-3, which on paper means every Arsenal player has a direct opponent, but they spent the game defending rather than pressing: 36% possession, only 159 passes in the opposition half to Arsenal's 335, and just 3 touches in the Arsenal box all match. Their 9 interceptions against Arsenal's 5 tells you they were sitting off, reading passing lanes and trying to spring forward rather than hunting the ball. Arsenal's answer was simply to keep the ball moving and stretch that back line — 8 corners, 10 shots from inside the box, and 36 touches in Coventry's penalty area meant Lampard's side were pinned in and never got the platform to counter.
explained.keyMoment: The 23rd minute. Havertz's opener on 15 already forced Coventry to chase the game, but Saka's second eight minutes later removed any incentive for them to come out, and the pattern was fixed for the next 70 minutes. Ødegaard's goal on 49 — assisted by Ben White, a full-back — was the same pattern simply repeating after the break.
explained.nerdCorner: Look at the one line that refuses to fit the story: big chances, 1 apiece. Coventry created exactly as many clear openings as Arsenal did, off 4 shots and 3 box touches — a wildly efficient use of their few moments forward. Arsenal's 1.88 xG was assembled from volume, not a single knockout opportunity: 20 shots, 8 corners, 36 box touches, and a 1 goalkeeper save total for Raya that flatters the defensive work as much as it describes it. The gap between xG 1.88 and xGOT 2.44 says the finishing outperformed the chances by a meaningful margin, which is the sort of thing that regresses. The process here — pinning a matching 4-3-3 in its own third and refusing to let it out — is far more repeatable than the conversion rate that turned it into 3-0.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper both teams lined up 4-3-3, but a team's shape on the teamsheet is only the shape they defend in. With the ball, an Arteta side like this usually slides one full-back inside next to the holding midfielder and pushes the other high, so the back four becomes a back three, two players screen in front of it, and five attackers spread across the last line. The movement of the full-backs — Calafiori and White here — is what turns one shape into the other, which is why a defender ends up credited with an assist.

lesson.explain: Both teams were recorded as 4-3-3, yet the game looked nothing like a mirror match — because 4-3-3 only describes how you defend. With the ball, this Arsenal side rearranges: a full-back tucks into midfield, the other pushes high, and the back four effectively becomes a back three feeding five attackers along the last line. That is why Calafiori and Ben White — both defenders on the teamsheet — are the two names credited with assists here, for Havertz on 15 and Ødegaard on 49. A defender producing the final pass is not a fluke; it is the shape doing what it is designed to do.

statTranslations.plain: Arsenal had the ball roughly two minutes in every three, so the shape you were watching for most of the afternoon was the in-possession one, not the 4-3-3.
Arsenal did more than twice as much of their passing inside Coventry's half, meaning the game was played almost entirely in one direction.
Arsenal got into the danger area a dozen times for every one time Coventry did — the clearest single measure of territorial control.
Arsenal's shots were worth roughly 1.88 goals by quality alone, but 2.44 once you account for where they were placed — the finishing was better than the chances.

statTranslations.stat: Shots 20 vs 4, shots inside box 10 vs 1
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal shot five times as often, and half their attempts came from inside the box, which is where shots actually get converted.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal scored after 23 seconds and never trailed. What the scoreline hides is that City had more of the ball, more shots and more touches in Arsenal's box — Arsenal won by creating four clear chances to City's one and putting them away.

shape.plainEnglish: Arsenal started 4-3-3 and City 4-2-3-1, but neither held that shape for long. With the ball Arsenal's left-back steps inside, which turns the back four into a back three and pushes five players onto the last line. Without the ball — which was most of this match — Arsenal folded into two compact banks of four and let City pass in front of them.

explained.opponentPlan: Maresca's City did what they were set up to do: 59% of the ball and 310 passes in Arsenal's half, against Arsenal's 110 in theirs. They got 34 touches in the Arsenal box to Arsenal's 27. What they could not do was turn any of that into a clear opening — one big chance all afternoon, and an xGOT of 0.34 says the few shots they did work were struck straight at Raya.
explained.keyMoment: The first goal, 23 seconds in. Lewis-Skelly found Calafiori for a finish before City had touched the ball. That one moment set the terms for everything after it: Arsenal could sit deep and defend a lead, and City had to come out, which is exactly the game Arsenal wanted.

lesson.explain: This is the match to learn it from, because the stats look like Arsenal lost. City had 59% of the ball, 12 shots to 9, and 34 touches in the box to 27. Arsenal deliberately gave all of that away: they dropped into two banks of four, defended the space in front of their own goal rather than chasing the ball, and made 16 tackles and 10 interceptions doing it. A low block concedes territory on purpose and bets that the opponent will never get a clean look at goal. City managed one big chance. Arsenal managed four.
lesson.spotIt: Next match, when Arsenal are ahead and the opponent has the ball, stop watching the ball and look at the shape. Two flat rows of four, squeezed into the width of the penalty area, with nobody chasing out to press — that is the low block doing its job, and it is not the same thing as being under pressure.

statTranslations.plain: The number that actually explains a 3-0. Arsenal made four genuinely clear openings; City made one.
Arsenal's chances were worth about 2.2 goals and City's about 1.1 — a real edge, but much closer than 3-0 suggests.
Where the match was won. Arsenal struck their shots far better than the chances deserved; City struck theirs far worse, firing straight at Raya.
Arsenal had well under half the ball and were entirely content with that.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in the opposition half: 110 vs 310
statTranslations.plain: City spent almost three times as much of the match camped in Arsenal's territory — and still lost 3-0.

explained.nerdCorner: The xG-to-xGOT gap is the whole story and it cuts both ways. Arsenal turned 2.16 xG into 2.53 xGOT — their finishing beat the quality of the chances. City turned 1.12 into 0.34, meaning their shooting was dreadful relative to the openings. That combined swing is worth roughly two and a half goals of finishing, and it is the least repeatable thing in football: expect both numbers to drift back toward their xG over a season. The more durable read is the big-chance count. Conceding 59% possession and 310 opposition-half passes while allowing exactly one clear sight of goal is a defensive structure working precisely as designed, and that part does repeat.
